content: 1. Post-treatment prophylaxis using component medicines with closely matched pharmacological properties is essential to minimize the risk of new infections that might encounter only a single drug. 2. The preferred drug regimen is one that can be administered as a single directly observed dose, rather than multi-day regimens. 3. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention, perennial malaria chemoprevention, or intermittent preventive treatment during pregnancy are examples of such approaches. 4. Mass drug administration (MDA) for Plasmodium vivax is particularly challenging because many infections involve dormant liver stages (hypnozoites), which cannot be eradicated without the use of an 8-aminoquinoline, the only class of drugs effective against hypnozoites. 5. Without the inclusion of an 8-aminoquinoline, a significant proportion of P. vivax cases treated in MDA programs will relapse within a few months. 6. Programs considering the use of medicines for radical cure of P. vivax must include testing for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency prior to treatment, establish effective pharmacovigilance systems, and ensure emergency access to blood transfusion services. 7. It is also critical to assess whether sufficient coverage and adherence to the full course of radical cure can be achieved. 8. A systematic review identified five cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) and six non-randomized studies (NRSs) across eight countries (Cambodia, India, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Panama, Solomon Islands, Venezuela, and Vietnam) that evaluated the impact of MDA on P. vivax transmission compared to no MDA. 9. None of the cRCTs and only one of the NRSs used sufficient dosages of an 8-aminoquinoline to achieve radical cure of P. vivax hypnozoites. 10. The time periods for results were grouped as 1–3 months, 4–12 months, and 12–24 months after the last round of MDA. 11. In the short term (1–3 months after MDA), MDA may reduce P. vivax prevalence, but the evidence is of low certainty. 12. The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of MDA on the incidence of P. vivax parasitemia and clinical malaria, with risk differences varying by transmission intensity. 13. In the medium term (4–12 months after MDA), MDA may result in little to no difference in P. vivax prevalence, with low-certainty evidence. 14. The evidence remains very uncertain about the effect of MDA on the incidence of P. vivax clinical malaria during this period. 15. In the long term (12–24 months after MDA), MDA may result in little to no difference in P. vivax prevalence, with low-certainty evidence. 16. Serious adverse events associated with MDA are likely minimal, with moderate-certainty evidence suggesting little to no difference in such events within 0–3 months or 4–12 months after MDA. 17. The GDG (Guideline Development Group) noted significant variability in the background levels of malaria transmission and other factors across the included studies, complicating the assessment of the balance of benefits and harms. 18. Only one NRS and no cRCTs used sufficient dosages of an 8-aminoquinoline for radical cure of P. vivax hypnozoites. 19. The GDG highlighted that the balance of effects might differ if radical cure of P. vivax was included in MDA, as preventing relapses through hypnozoite treatment could enhance the impact of MDA but also increase potential harms, particularly in G6PD-deficient individuals. 20. The inclusion of G6PD testing, pharmacovigilance systems, and emergency blood transfusion services would likely reduce acceptability and feasibility due to increased complexity. 21. The GDG judged that the available evidence on the benefits and harms of including radical cure in MDA for P. vivax was limited, and the overall certainty of the evidence was very low. 22. The GDG concluded that the balance of effects did not favor either MDA or no MDA for reducing P. vivax transmission. 23. The GDG expressed concern about the reduced long-term effectiveness of MDA for P. vivax without the use of an 8-aminoquinoline and the increased complexity of safely administering these drugs. 24. The resources required for MDA implementation were judged to be substantial and could negatively impact the implementation of other recommended malaria strategies. 25. While cost-effectiveness data were limited, the GDG judged that MDA was likely cost-effective for reducing P. vivax transmission, depending on the time period over which it was measured and whether elimination was achieved. 26. The acceptability of MDA was judged to vary depending on stakeholder groups, prior experiences with MDA, and whether radical cure with an 8-aminoquinoline was included. 27. Feasibility was judged to depend on the population size to be covered and the inclusion of radical cure, which requires G6PD testing, pharmacovigilance systems, and emergency blood transfusion services. 28. The GDG proposed a conditional recommendation for the use of MDA for P. vivax, particularly if it could rapidly reduce transmission to enable intensive surveillance activities. 29. Further research is needed to evaluate the impact, acceptability, feasibility, and potential harms of MDA for P. vivax, including the safe provision of 8-aminoquinolines as part of radical cure. 30. Research should also determine the optimal timing, number of MDA rounds, and minimum effective coverage to maximize the impact of MDA on P. vivax. 31. The GDG emphasized the need to assess whether geographical isolation or population mobility modifies the impact of MDA on P. vivax transmission. 32. Barriers to MDA implementation include absenteeism, seasonal mobility, and challenges in determining the optimal timing of campaigns due to weather, agricultural activities, and religious events. 33. Community engagement, education, and support from local authorities are critical to improving MDA acceptability and adherence. 34. The inclusion of an 8-aminoquinoline in MDA for radical cure may negatively affect acceptability due to safety concerns and the long treatment period required. 35. The GDG concluded that MDA could be a useful intervention if it effectively reduces P. vivax transmission quickly, enabling the initiation of intensive surveillance activities.
